sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale (IA, non relue par un helleniste), realisee a partir du texte grec zoo24/2g (edition Littre, 30 chapitres, 37 a 66), chapitre par chapitre, en verifiant chaque passage par comparaison avec la traduction anglaise publiee de reference (Loeb Classical Library, W.H.S. Jones, 1931, Hippocrates vol. IV) sans la recopier ni la paraphraser etroitement, cette derniere restant protegee par le droit d'auteur americain jusqu'au 1er janvier 2027 (regle des 95 ans). Les numeros de chapitre (attribut n des div de type "chapter") reprennent ceux de l'edition Littre, identiques a zoo24/2g et a la pagination Loeb. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un helleniste specialiste avant toute citation savante.

div.p: Here is how one should judge the lie and character of any given region. As a general rule, a district facing south is hotter and drier than one facing north, since it lies closer to the sun. In such regions the races of men, and the plants that grow from the earth, must necessarily be drier, hotter and stronger than in the opposite regions - compare, for instance, the Libyan race with the Pontic, and those nearest to each. Regions considered in themselves are as follows: high, parched land lying toward the south is drier than plains similarly situated, because it holds less moisture - such land does not retain rainwater, whereas plains do. Marshland and bogs produce both moisture and warmth in the body: warmth, since such ground is sunken and shut in on all sides with no air circulating through it; moisture, since whatever grows out of such soil, and feeds the local inhabitants, is itself wetter, and the very air breathed there is denser owing to the standing water. Waterless hollows, by contrast, produce dryness together with warmth: warmth for the same reason, being sunken and enclosed; dryness both because the food grown there is dry and because the air breathed, itself dry, draws moisture from our bodies for its own nourishment, lacking any wetter source nearby to draw on instead. Where mountains lie to the south of a district, the south winds that reach it are parching and unhealthy; where mountains lie to the north, the north winds there cause disturbance and sickness. Where hollow ground lies to the north of a town, or where an island lies opposite it out at sea, that district turns hot and unhealthy under the summer winds, since no north wind passes through to sweep in clean air, and the summer winds bring it no relief from heat. Of islands, those near the mainland have harsher winters, while those far out to sea are milder in winter, because on the mainland the snow and ice remain in place and send cold winds on to the neighboring islands, whereas open sea does not hold snow and ice through the winter.

Concerning winds, one must discern their nature and power as follows. All winds by nature moisten and cool the bodies of living creatures and the plants that grow from the earth, for this reason: all these winds necessarily blow from snow, ice, heavy frosts, rivers, lakes, or ground that has become wet and cold. The stronger winds come from larger and more intense such sources, the weaker from lesser and less intense ones; for just as animals possess breath, so does everything else, some less, some in proportion to their size. All winds, then, by nature cool and moisten. But because of the position of places and districts through which winds travel to reach each region, they come to differ from one another - some colder, some hotter, some moister, some drier, some more unhealthy, some more healthy. The reason for each must be understood as follows: the north wind blows cold and moist because it sets out from, and travels through, such regions as the sun does not reach, nor does it, by drying the air, draw off the moisture; so it arrives over the inhabited world keeping its own power, except where the lie of the land corrupts it - and it is coldest for those who dwell nearest its source, least cold for those farthest away. The south wind blows from regions of the same nature as the north wind - for, blowing from the southern pole, setting out from abundant snow, ice, and heavy frost, it must necessarily blow, for those who dwell close to that region, in the same way that the north wind blows for us. But by the time it reaches every region it no longer arrives the same: passing near the sun's path and blowing under the midday heat, its moisture is drawn off by the sun; and being dried, it grows rarefied - hence it necessarily becomes hot and dry by the time it arrives here. In the nearest regions, then, it necessarily yields such a hot, dry power, and this it does in Libya: it shrivels the growing things, and dries out the people without their noticing; for having no moisture to draw from sea or river, it draws its moisture instead from the animals and the growing things. But once it has crossed the sea, being hot and rarefied, it fills the land it strikes with abundant moisture; so the south wind must be hot and moist, except where the lie of particular places is responsible for otherwise. The other winds behave likewise according to their sources. As for how the winds behave in each region: a wind reaching a district from the sea, or carrying the character of snow, ice, lakes, or rivers, brings coolness and wetness to plant and animal alike, and is healthful to the body so long as its coldness is not extreme; taken to excess, though, it can cause harm, by swinging the body sharply between hot and cold - an affliction familiar to those settled near great rivers in marshy, warm country. Winds from these same sources, kept within bounds, do good instead, supplying clean, unadulterated air and feeding moisture to the body's inborn heat. A wind that forms over dry land, however, comes drier by necessity, robbed of moisture by both sun and soil; finding no reservoir to feed on, it turns instead to living creatures for its moisture, doing harm to plant and beast alike. And winds that come pouring over mountains into cities not only dry the body but disturb the very breath we draw in, and disturb men's bodies, so as to bring on sickness. Such, then, is the nature and power of each; how one should prepare oneself against each I shall show as the account proceeds.

Concerning the power of foods and drinks, both what is natural to each and what results from preparation, one must know as follows. Those who have undertaken to make sweeping statements about the power of sweet things, or fatty things, or salty things, or anything else of that kind, do not judge rightly; for sweet things do not all have the same power as one another, nor do fatty things, nor anything else of that sort - many sweet things loosen the bowels, others bind them, others dry, others moisten. The same holds for everything else: some things are astringent and yet loosen the bowels and promote urine, others do neither. So too with things that heat, and with everything else - one thing has one power, another a different one. It is not possible, then, to state in general terms what sort of thing each is; but I shall teach, case by case, what power each possesses.

Barley by nature is cold and moist, and it also dries; it likewise possesses a certain purgative quality drawn from the juice of the husk. Here is the proof: if you boil unhulled barley, its broth purges strongly; but if the barley has been hulled, the broth cools more and binds the bowels instead. Once roasted, the moist, purgative part is driven off by the fire, leaving only the cold, dry part. Whatever needs cooling and drying is achieved by using barley-meal made into various kinds of barley-cake; and the cake's own power is as follows. Meal that has not been sifted gives less nourishment but loosens the bowels more; the sifted, pure meal is more nourishing but loosens less. A barley-cake that is well kneaded, sprinkled with water, unworked and light, both loosens the bowels and cools: it cools because it has been moistened with cold water; it loosens the bowels because it is digested quickly; it is light because much of its substance is expelled together with wind. For the passages, being narrow, cannot admit more nourishment once already occupied: what is rarefied together with the wind is expelled outward, while what remains produces flatulence - part rising as belching, part passing downward - so that much of the nourishment is breathed away from the body. But if you knead the cake and give it at once, freshly mixed, such a cake is drying: for the meal, being dry and only just made moist by the water, on reaching the stomach draws off its heat-bearing moisture - since it is the nature of the hot to draw the cold, and the cold to draw the hot; and as the moisture in the stomach is used up, drying necessarily follows, while the water brought in with the cake, being cold, brings its own cooling as well. So whatever needs drying or cooling, whether affected by diarrhoea or by some other heat, is treated by a cake of this kind. Cake that has been thoroughly worked and kneaded dry does not dry as much, because it has been pressed very firmly together; but it gives the body the most nourishment, since the passages, being gently dissolved, admit the nourishment gradually - it therefore passes the bowels slowly, produces no flatulence, and causes no belching. Cake that is well worked but freshly kneaded nourishes less, loosens the bowels more, and produces more flatulence.

Barley-water made with meal alone: taken with water it cools and nourishes; with wine it warms, nourishes, and binds; with honey it warms less and nourishes, but loosens the bowels more, unless the honey is unmixed - in which case it does not loosen but binds instead. Taken with milk, all kinds nourish, but not equally: ewe's milk binds, goat's milk loosens more, cow's milk less, while mare's and ass's milk loosen more still. Wheat is stronger than barley and more nourishing, but loosens the bowels less, both the grain itself and its broth. Bread made from unsifted flour dries and loosens the bowels, while bread from the pure, sifted flour nourishes more but loosens less. Of breads themselves, leavened bread is light and loosens the bowels: it is light because the moisture - which is its nourishment - has already been used up by the sour leaven; it loosens because it is quickly digested. Unleavened bread loosens less but nourishes more.

Bread kneaded with broth is lighter still, nourishes adequately, and loosens the bowels: it nourishes because it is pure, it is light because it has been kneaded and leavened and baked with the lightest of ingredients, and it loosens because it is mixed with the sweet, loosening quality of the wheat. Among breads, the largest loaves are the most nourishing, because their moisture is least burned away by the fire; and oven-baked loaves are more nourishing than those baked on a griddle or a spit, because they are less scorched by the fire. Loaves baked in a covered pan, and those baked buried in embers, are the driest - the one kind because of the ash, the other because the moisture is drawn off by the earthenware. Loaves of fine wheat-flour are the strongest of all these, and those made from groats even more so, and highly nourishing, though they do not loosen the bowels to the same degree. Pure wheat-flour taken in water cools, and so does the wash of raw dough. Boiled bran-water is light and loosens the bowels. Flour dishes boiled in milk loosen the bowels more than those boiled in water, on account of the whey, especially in dishes meant to be loosening. Whatever is made from flour boiled or baked with honey and oil is heating and productive of belching: productive of belching because, being nourishing, such food does not loosen the bowels; heating because, being fatty and sweet and made of ingredients unsuited to one another, requiring different degrees of cooking, yet combined together. Fine flour and groats when boiled are strong and nourishing, but do not loosen the bowels.

Emmer and one-seeded wheat are lighter than wheat, and the products made from them resemble those made from wheat, though they loosen the bowels more. Oats, whether eaten or made into gruel, moisten and cool.

Freshly ground barley-meal and wheat-flour are drier than when aged, because they are nearer to the fire and to their preparation; with age, the heat they held breathes away and cold takes its place. Hot bread dries, cold bread less so, stale bread less still, though it produces a certain wasting.

Beans are somewhat nourishing, binding, and productive of flatulence: they produce flatulence because the passages do not readily admit their warm-arriving nourishment; they bind because their residue is small. Peas cause less flatulence but loosen the bowels more. Pale chickpeas and long beans loosen the bowels more than these, cause less flatulence, and are nourishing. White chickpeas loosen the bowels, promote urine, and nourish - the fleshy part nourishes, the sweet part promotes urine, the salty part loosens the bowels. Groats and husks of millet are dry and binding, but strong food for laborers when eaten with figs; millet itself, boiled, is nourishing, though it does not loosen the bowels. Lentils are heating and disturbing, neither loosening the bowels nor binding them. Vetch is binding and strong, thickens the body, fills it out, and gives a good complexion. Flaxseed is nourishing and binding, with a certain cooling quality as well. Clary seed acts much like flax. Lupins are by nature strong and hot, but through preparation become lighter, more cooling, and loosen the bowels. Hedge-mustard moistens and loosens the bowels. Cucumber seed promotes urine more than it loosens the bowels. Unwashed sesame loosens the bowels, fills out and thickens the body: it loosens because of its outer husk, and fills and thickens because of its flesh; washed sesame loosens less, but thickens and fills more, while drying and producing heat because of its oiliness and fatness. Safflower loosens the bowels. Poppy is binding, especially the black poppy, though the white as well; it is nourishing and strong. Of all these, the juices loosen the bowels more than the solid flesh does; one must therefore manage their preparation accordingly - for drying purposes, remove the juice and use the solid part; for loosening the bowels, use more of the juice and less of the flesh, choosing the flesh richest in juice.

Concerning the flesh of animals eaten as food, one must know as follows. Beef is strong, binding, and hard for the stomach to digest, because this animal has thick, abundant blood, and its flesh is heavy for the body, as are its very flesh, its blood, and its milk. In animals whose milk is thin and whose blood is correspondingly thin, the flesh is likewise similar. Goat's flesh is lighter than beef and loosens the bowels more. Pork gives the body more strength than either of these, and loosens the bowels adequately, because the pig has thin, blood-poor veins but abundant flesh. Lamb is lighter than mutton, and kid lighter than goat's flesh, because they contain less blood and more moisture; for animals that are by nature dry and strong loosen the bowels while still young and tender, but not in the same way once grown - and veal behaves the same way in relation to beef. Piglet's flesh is heavier than that of grown swine: for this animal, being by nature fleshy and poor in blood, has an excess of moisture while still young; so when the passages cannot admit the nourishment as it arrives, it remains within, produces heat, and disturbs the bowels. Donkey meat loosens the bowels, foal's meat still more, while horsemeat is lighter. Dog's flesh heats, dries, and gives strength, but does not loosen the bowels; puppy's flesh moistens and loosens the bowels, and promotes urine still more. Wild boar's flesh dries, gives strength, and loosens the bowels. Venison dries, loosens the bowels less, but promotes urine more. Hare is dry and binding, though it promotes urine somewhat. Fox's flesh is moister, and also promotes urine; and land hedgehog's flesh promotes urine and moistens.

Concerning birds: nearly all birds are drier than four-footed animals; for whatever has no bladder neither urinates nor produces saliva, and is therefore altogether dry - because, on account of the heat of its stomach, the body's moisture is consumed as nourishment by that heat, so that neither urination nor salivation occurs; and whatever lacks such moisture must necessarily be dry. The driest flesh, then, appears to be that of the wood-pigeon; second the domestic pigeon; third partridge, cock, and turtle-dove; the moistest is goose. Grain-eating birds are drier than the rest. Duck, and all birds that live among marshes or in water, are entirely moist.

Among fish, the driest are these: scorpion-fish, weaver-fish, stargazer, gurnard, grey wrasse, perch, and shad. Light are almost all the rock-fish, such as thrush-wrasse, another wrasse, sprat, and goby; these, and the ones just named, are lighter than the wandering fish - for by staying still they keep their flesh loose and light. Fish that wander and are buffeted by the waves, worn down by exertion, have firmer, denser flesh. Torpedo-fish, skate, and plaice, and the like, are lighter still. Fish that take their nourishment in muddy, watery places, such as grey mullet, another kind of mullet, and eels, are heavier, because they draw their nourishment from the water, the mud, and the things that grow in such places - and the very air that rises from these fish into a man harms him and weighs him down. River fish and lake fish are heavier still than these. Octopus and cuttlefish, and the like, are neither light, as is commonly thought, nor do they loosen the bowels; they also dull the eyesight - though their broth does loosen the bowels. As for shellfish, such as the fan-mussel, purple-shell, limpet, whelk, and oyster, the flesh itself is drying, though their broth loosens the bowels. Mussels, scallops, and small clams loosen the bowels even more than these; sea-anemones most of all; and cartilaginous fish moisten and loosen the bowels. Of sea-urchins, the roe, and the juice of the crayfish, loosen the bowels, as do river-crabs and sea-crabs - the river kind more than the sea kind - and they also promote urine. Salt-fish dry and cause wasting, though the fatty kinds loosen the bowels reasonably well. Of salt-fish, the driest are those from the sea, second those from rivers, and moistest those from lakes; among the sea fish themselves, the so-called perch is the driest, both fresh and salted.

Among domesticated animals, those that range over woodland and open country are drier than those kept indoors, because exertion dries them through exposure to sun and cold, and because they breathe drier air. Wild animals are drier than tame ones; raw-flesh eaters drier than browsers; those that eat little drier than those that eat much; grass-eaters that feed on fresh green fodder are drier than other grazers, and fruit-eaters drier than non-fruit-eaters; those that drink little are drier than those that drink much; those with abundant blood are drier than the bloodless or blood-poor; animals in their prime are drier than the very old or the very young; males are drier than females; the intact are drier than the castrated; dark-coated animals are drier than pale ones, and shaggy ones drier than smooth ones - the opposite conditions producing moister flesh in each case. Among the flesh of these animals itself, the strongest is that which works hardest and has the most blood, and that on which the animal lies down to rest; the lightest flesh is that which works least, has the least blood, comes from parts kept in shade, and lies deepest within the animal. Among the bloodless parts, brain and marrow are the strongest; the lightest are heads, mussels, scallops, and feet. Among fish, the upper parts are driest, the underbelly lightest, and the head moistest of all, on account of its fat and its brain.

Birds' eggs possess something strong, nourishing, and productive of flatulence: strong, because they are the origin of the animal; nourishing, because the egg serves as milk to the chick; productive of flatulence, because from a small bulk it expands into a great one.

Cheese is strong, heating, nourishing, and binding: strong because it is very close to the source of life; nourishing because it is the fleshy residue of milk; heating because it is fatty; binding because it has been made to set by fig-juice and rennet.

Water is cold and moist; wine is hot and dry, and possesses a certain purgative quality drawn from its material. Among wines, the dark, astringent ones are driest, and neither loosen the bowels, nor promote urine, nor are spat up; they dry by their heat, using up the body's moisture. The soft dark wines are moister, cause flatulence, and loosen the bowels more. The sweet dark wines are moister still and weaker, and cause flatulence by introducing moisture. Pale, astringent wines heat but do not dry, and promote urine more than they loosen the bowels. Young wines loosen the bowels more than old, because they are nearer to the state of must and more nourishing; and among wines of the same age, the fragrant loosen more than the odourless, being riper, and the thick more than the thin. Thin wines promote urine more; and pale, thin, sweet wines promote urine more than they loosen the bowels, while cooling, reducing, and moistening the body, weakening the blood, and increasing whatever opposes the blood in the body. Must causes flatulence, disturbs the stomach, and moves the bowels: it causes flatulence because it heats, it moves the bowels because it purges, and it disturbs by fermenting and loosening within the stomach. Sour wines cool, reduce, and moisten: they cool and reduce by emptying the body of moisture, and they moisten from the water taken in together with the wine. Vinegar has a cooling effect, since it consumes the body's moisture by dissolving it, and it binds the bowels more than it loosens them, being unnourishing and sharp. Boiled-down wine heats, moistens, and moves the bowels: it heats because it retains the character of wine, it moistens because it is nourishing, and it moves the bowels because it is sweet and has been boiled down. The lees of pressed grapes moisten, move the bowels, and cause flatulence, for the same reason that must does.
Honey, unmixed, is hot and dry; mixed with water it moistens and loosens the bowels in the bilious, but binds them in the phlegmatic. Sweet wine loosens the bowels more in the phlegmatic.

Concerning vegetables, matters stand as follows. Garlic is hot; it loosens the bowels and promotes urine, and is good for the body, though harmful to the eyes - for by purging the body strongly it dulls the sight; it loosens the bowels and promotes urine because of its purgative quality; boiled it is weaker than raw; it produces flatulence by obstructing the passage of wind. Onion is good for the eyesight but bad for the body, since it is hot and produces a burning sensation, and does not loosen the bowels; it gives the body no nourishment or benefit, and by its heat it dries, on account of its acrid juice. Leek heats less, promotes urine, and loosens the bowels; it has a certain purgative quality, moistens, and stops sour belching; it is good to eat last, after other foods. Radish moistens, dispersing phlegm by its pungency, though its leaves do so less, except for sufferers from arthritic complaints; the root is troublesome, tending to float on the stomach and being hard to digest. Cress is hot and dissolves the flesh, and checks white phlegm, so as to bring on strangury. Mustard is hot and loosens the bowels, though it too makes urination difficult; rocket behaves much the same way. Coriander is hot and binding, and stops sour belching; eaten last it induces sleep. Lettuce is rather cold before it has developed its milky juice, and produces a certain weakness in the body. Dill is hot and binding, and stops sneezing when smelled. Celery promotes urine more than it loosens the bowels, and its roots do so even more than the plant itself. Basil is dry, hot, and binding. Rue promotes urine more than it loosens the bowels, has an astringent quality, and taken beforehand helps against harmful drugs. Asparagus is dry and binding. Sage is dry and binding. Nightshade is cooling and prevents nocturnal emissions. Purslane cools while fresh, but warms when preserved in salt. Nettle purges. Calamint heats and purges. Mint heats, promotes urine, and stops vomiting; but if eaten often it dissolves the seed so that it flows away, hinders erection, and weakens the body. Dock heats and loosens the bowels. Orache is moist but does not loosen the bowels. Blite is not hot, but loosens the bowels. Cabbage heats, loosens the bowels, and expels bile. Of beet, the juice loosens the bowels, but the leaf eaten as a vegetable binds them, while the roots loosen the bowels even more than the leaf. Colocynth cools, moistens, and loosens the bowels, but does not promote urine. Turnip is heating, moistens and disturbs the body, does not loosen the bowels, and makes urination difficult. Pennyroyal heats and loosens the bowels. Marjoram heats and expels bile. Savory acts much like marjoram. Thyme is hot, loosens the bowels and promotes urine, and expels phlegm. Hyssop heats and expels phlegm. Among wild vegetables, those that are heating and fragrant to the taste heat the body and promote urine more than they loosen the bowels; those of a moist, cold, insipid nature, or of heavy odour, loosen the bowels more than they promote urine; those that are astringent or harsh are binding; those that are pungent and fragrant promote urine; those that are pungent and dry to the taste all dry the body; those that are sour have a cooling effect. Diuretic juices are those of samphire, celery, and steeped garlic, of laburnum, fennel, leek, maidenhair fern, and nightshade; cooling are hart's-tongue fern, mint, hartwort, chicory, bur-parsley, St. John's wort, and nettle; loosening and purgative are chickpea, lentil, barley, beet, cabbage, mercury, elder, and safflower - all of these loosen the bowels more than they promote urine.

Concerning fruit, matters stand as follows. Tree fruit loosens the bowels more than the rest, and fresh fruit more than dried. Their several powers will now be given. Mulberries heat, moisten, and loosen the bowels. Ripe pears heat, moisten, and loosen the bowels, but hard pears are binding; ripe wild pears in winter loosen the bowels and purge the stomach, while unripe ones bind. Sweet apples are hard to digest, sour and half-ripe ones less so; quinces are astringent and do not loosen the bowels; the juice of apples is binding against vomiting and promotes urine, as does their scent against vomiting; wild apples are binding, though boiled and eaten they loosen the bowels more; for shortness of breath both their juice and the fruit itself, taken as drink, are helpful. Sorb-apples, medlars, cornel-cherries, and other such fruit are binding and astringent. The juice of the sweet pomegranate loosens the bowels, though it carries a certain burning quality; wine-flavoured pomegranates cause flatulence; sour ones are more cooling; the seeds of all kinds are binding. Raw cucumbers are cold and hard to digest; ripe ones promote urine and loosen the bowels, but cause flatulence. Grapes are hot, moist, and loosen the bowels, especially the pale ones; sweet grapes heat strongly, since they already contain much heat; unripe, sour grapes heat less, and purge when drunk as juice; raisins produce a burning sensation but loosen the bowels. Green figs moisten, loosen the bowels, and heat: they moisten because they are full of juice, they heat on account of their sweet sap, and they loosen the bowels as well; the first figs of the season are the worst, being fullest of sap, while the last are the best; dried figs produce a burning sensation but loosen the bowels. Almonds cause a burning sensation but are nourishing: they burn on account of their oil, and nourish on account of their flesh. Round nuts act much the same way; flat nuts, when ripe, are nourishing, and loosen the bowels when their skin is removed, though they cause flatulence; their inner skins are binding. Acorns of the holm-oak, common acorns, and beech-mast are binding whether raw or roasted, less so when boiled.

Fatty meats produce a burning sensation but loosen the bowels. Salted meat preserved in wine dries and nourishes: it dries because of the wine, and nourishes because of the flesh; preserved in vinegar it heats less, because of the vinegar, but nourishes adequately; salted meat preserved in brine is less nourishing, since the salt has robbed it of moisture, though it causes wasting, dries, and loosens the bowels adequately. One must remove or add to the powers of each food in the following way, knowing that all things - both animals and plants - are composed by fire and water, and are made to grow by these, and are resolved back into them. For strong foods, then, one removes their power by repeated boiling and cooling; for moist foods, one draws off the moisture by roasting and toasting; for dry foods, by soaking and moistening; for salty foods, by soaking and boiling; for bitter and pungent foods, by mixing them with sweet ones; for astringent foods, with oily ones - and one should reason about everything else on the same principles already stated. Foods that have been roasted or toasted are more binding than raw ones, because the fire has removed their moisture, their sap, and their oiliness; so when such food falls into the stomach, it draws moisture out of the stomach itself, closing up the mouths of the small veins as it dries and heats them, and so it checks the passages of moisture. Everything grown in waterless, dry, stifling places is drier, hotter, and gives the body more strength, because, bulk for bulk, it is heavier, denser, and richer in substance than what grows in moist, well-watered, cool ground - which is moister, lighter, and cooler. One must therefore learn the power not only of the food, drink, or animal itself, but also of the country it comes from. When one wishes to bring stronger nourishment to the body from the same kinds of food, one should use grain, drink, and animals from waterless regions; when lighter and moister nourishment is wanted, one should use those from well-watered regions. Sweet, pungent, salty, bitter, astringent, and fleshy foods all tend by nature to heat, whether dry or moist. Those among them with the greater share of dryness dry and heat; those with the greater share of moisture heat while moistening, and loosen the bowels more than the dry foods do - for by giving more nourishment to the body, they draw it back toward the stomach, and in moistening they loosen the bowels. Foods or drinks that heat throughout and yet dry, without producing spitting, urination, or loosening of the bowels, dry the body for this reason: the body, being heated, is emptied of its moisture - part used up by the food itself, part consumed as nourishment by the soul's own heat, part driven out through the skin as it is heated and rarefied. Sweet, fat, and oily foods are filling, because from a small bulk they yield abundant substance; being heated and diffused, they fill the body's heat and produce a sense of calm. Sour, pungent, astringent, harsh, coarse, and dry foods do not fill the body, because they open and cleanse the mouths of the veins; some by drying, some by biting, some by their astringency, they cause the moisture in the flesh to shrink and contract into a small bulk, so that much empty space is left in the body. So whenever you wish to fill the body from little food, or to empty it from much, use foods of this kind. Fresh foods of every sort give more strength than others, because they are nearer to the living state; stale and spoiled foods loosen the bowels more than fresh ones, because they are nearer to putrefaction. Half-cooked food causes griping and belching, because what needs to be worked upon by fire is instead left to the stomach to manage, though the stomach is weaker than what it receives. Dishes prepared with rich sauces are heating and moist, because, being oily, fiery, and hot, and possessing powers unsuited to one another, they nonetheless settle together in the same place. Dishes prepared in brine or vinegar are better, and do not produce a burning sensation.

Concerning baths, matters stand as follows. Fresh water moistens and cools, for it gives moisture to the body; salt-water bathing heats and dries, since, being by nature hot, it draws moisture out of the body. Hot baths, taken on an empty stomach, reduce and cool the body: they carry off its moisture by their heat, and as the flesh is emptied of moisture the body grows cool; but taken after eating, they heat and moisten, spreading the body's existing moisture through a greater bulk. Cold baths do the opposite: to an empty body they impart a certain warmth, being themselves cold; but taken after eating, they draw off moisture while it is still moist and leave dryness, filling the body instead with what dryness it already had. Failure to bathe dries the body as its moisture is consumed, and so, likewise, does failure to anoint oneself with oil.

Oil heats, moistens, and softens. Sun and fire dry for this reason: being hot and dry, they draw moisture out of the body. Shade and mild cold have a moistening effect instead, since what they release exceeds what they draw off. All sweating, as it departs the body, both dries and reduces it, since moisture leaves the body along with it. Sexual intercourse reduces, moistens, and heats the body: it heats through the exertion and the discharge of moisture; it reduces through the resulting emptiness; and it moistens because of what remains in the body from the dissolution brought on by the exertion.

Vomiting reduces the body through the emptying of its nourishment, though it does not dry it - unless one fails to treat it properly the following day - but rather moistens it more, through the fullness and dissolution of flesh that exertion brings; if, however, one allows this dissolved matter to be used up the next day as nourishment by the body's heat, and gently resumes one's regimen, it does dry the body. Vomiting relieves a bowel that has become constipated, and checks one that is loosening beyond due measure - in the one case by moistening it further, in the other by drying it. So when you wish to check the bowels, you should induce vomiting as soon as possible after eating, before the food has had time to become moistened and drawn down into the body, and one should rely more on astringent and harsh foods; but when you wish to relieve the bowels, it is advantageous to let the food linger as long as possible, and to use pungent, salty, oily, and sweet foods and drinks.

Sleep on an empty stomach reduces and cools the body, provided it is not prolonged, by emptying it of its existing moisture; but if prolonged beyond measure, it heats the body further, dissolving the flesh, weakening the body, and rendering it feeble; taken after eating, it heats and moistens, spreading the nourishment through the body. Sleep after a morning walk dries the body most of all. Wakefulness harms a man who has eaten, by preventing the food from being properly dissolved; in one who has not eaten, it brings on a certain reduction, but does less harm. Idleness moistens and weakens the body, for the soul, remaining still, does not use up the body's moisture; exertion, by contrast, dries the body and makes it strong. Eating only once a day reduces and dries the body and checks the bowels, because the body's moisture, both in the bowels and in the flesh, is consumed by the soul's own heat; two meals a day produce the opposite effect. Water taken as drink reduces the body whether hot or cold. Excessive cold, whether of air, food, or drink, congeals the body's moisture and constricts the bowels through this congealing and chilling, for it overpowers the soul's own moisture. Likewise, excess of heat, in turn, also congeals, and to such a degree that no diffusion can take place. Whatever heats the body without providing nourishment, without emptying the flesh of moisture and without excess, brings on a chill in a man; for as the body's existing moisture is emptied out, it becomes filled instead with air drawn in from without, and so grows cold.

Concerning exertions, I shall now explain what power each possesses. Some are natural, others forced; among the natural ones are the exertion of sight, of hearing, of speech, and of anxious thought. The power of sight is as follows: the soul, attending to what it sees, is set in motion and heated; being heated, it dries, as its moisture is used up. Through hearing, when a sound falls upon it, the soul is shaken and made to labour; labouring, it heats and dries. Whatever a man turns over anxiously in his mind sets his soul in motion, heating and drying it; and as it uses up the body's moisture in this labour, it empties the flesh and makes the man thin. As for exertions of the voice - such as speaking, reading aloud, or singing - all of these set the soul in motion; and being so moved, it dries and heats, and uses up the moisture within the body.

Walking is a natural exercise, and indeed the most natural of all the rest, yet it involves a certain forcing of the body. The power of each kind of walk is as follows. A walk after dinner dries both the bowels and the body, and prevents the belly from growing fat, for this reason: as the man moves, both his body and his food grow warm; the flesh then draws off the moisture, and does not allow it to gather about the stomach - so the body as a whole fills out, while the belly grows thinner. The drying happens because motion warms the body, and in that warmth the food's finest component is spent - some of it burned up by the body's own inner heat, some breathed out, some carried off as urine - leaving behind only the driest residue of what was eaten, so that both bowels and flesh end up parched. A morning walk likewise reduces the body, and it makes the region about the head light, clear, and quick of hearing, and it relieves the bowels: it reduces the body because, as the body moves, it grows warm, and its moisture is thinned and purged away - part through the breath, part through blowing the nose and clearing the throat, part consumed as nourishment by the soul's own heat; it relieves the bowels because, the bowels being warm, when cold air falls upon them from above, the warmth yields ground to the cold. It makes the head light for this reason: once the bowels are emptied, being warm, they draw moisture to themselves both from the rest of the body and from the head; and as the head is emptied, both sight and hearing are cleared, and men become keen-sighted. Walks taken after exercise render the body clean, and reduce it, since they do not allow the dissolved matter produced by exertion to settle, but instead purge it away.

Of runs, the long, winding kind, gradually built up from a short distance, by heating the flesh, can help digest and dissolve it, and thoroughly work the power of food already present in the flesh; they render the body slower and heavier than sprinting does, and suit those who eat much, and are more useful in winter than in summer. Running while wrapped in a cloak has the same power, but heats more thoroughly, and makes the body moister, though also more sallow, since the pure air striking the body is not allowed to cleanse it, but is instead re-breathed within the same enclosed air; this therefore suits those who are dry and overly fleshy, and anyone wishing to reduce his flesh, as well as older people, on account of their bodily coldness. Double-course runs, and runs of the sort used to train race-horses at speed, dissolve the flesh less, but reduce the body more, because, the exertion lying outside the parts governed by the soul, it draws moisture away from the flesh and thins and dries the body. Sprinting dissolves the flesh least of all, but reduces it, and above all contracts the flesh and the bowels, because, using the most rapid breathing, it draws the body's moisture to itself with the greatest speed.

Sudden, violent, jerking movements are unsuitable for those who are dry, for they cause strains, for the following reason: the body, having been thoroughly heated, has its skin greatly thinned, while its flesh is compacted less than by sprint-training, and its flesh is emptied of moisture. Gentle swaying and lifting movements scarcely heat the flesh at all, but stimulate the body and the soul, and empty it of breath. Wrestling and rubbing bring on exertion felt more on the body's surface; they heat the flesh, make it firm, and cause it to grow, for the following reason: parts that are by nature solid become compacted by rubbing, while hollow parts - wherever there are veins - grow larger; for as the flesh is heated and dried it draws nourishment to itself through the veins, and so grows. Rolling in the dust acts much like wrestling, but dries more, because of the dust, and builds flesh less. Exercise of the fingertips reduces the body and draws the flesh upward; punch-ball exercise and arm-swinging produce much the same effect. Holding the breath can force open the pores, thin the skin, and drive moisture out through it.

Exercise in the dust and exercise in oil differ as follows: dust is cold, oil is hot. In winter, oil is more conducive to growth, because the cold hinders the moisture from leaving the body; in summer, oil, by producing an excess of heat, melts the flesh away, especially when the body is already overheated by the season, by the oil, and by the exertion itself. Dust, in summer, is more conducive to growth, since by cooling the body it prevents it from being overheated to excess; in winter, however, it has a chilling, frost-like effect. Lingering in the dust after exercise in summer is beneficial for a short while, by its cooling effect, but for long periods it dries the body excessively and renders it hard and wooden. Rubbing with oil and water softens the body, and does not allow it to be violently overheated.

Concerning the fatigue that arises in the body, matters stand as follows. Untrained men grow fatigued from any exertion at all, since no part of their body has been worked to meet any kind of effort; trained bodies grow fatigued from unaccustomed exertions, and are fatigued also by their habitual exercises, when these are carried to excess. Such, then, are the kinds of fatigue; their nature is as follows. Untrained men, having moist flesh, when they exert themselves, their body being heated, release a great quantity of dissolved matter; whatever is sweated out, or purged away together with the breath, causes no further trouble beyond the mere emptying of the body from its accustomed state; but whatever of this dissolved matter remains within causes trouble not only to the part of the body thus emptied against habit, but also to the part that receives the moisture - for it is not akin to the body's nourishment, but hostile to it. Into fleshless parts of the body it does not settle in the same way, but into fleshy parts it does, so that it causes trouble to these until it departs. Since it has no circulation, remaining motionless it heats itself and whatever it touches; and if a great quantity of it is separated out in this way, it overpowers even the healthy part, so that the whole body is heated together, and a strong fever is produced. For once the blood has been heated and drawn upon, it quickens the circulation of what is in the body, and the rest of the body is purged by the breath, while the compacted matter, being heated, is thinned and driven together out of the flesh onto the skin, which is called hot sweat. Once this has been separated off, the blood settles back into its natural state, the fever subsides, and the fatigue ceases, generally on the third day. Such fatigue should be treated as follows: dissolve the compacted matter with steam-baths and hot baths, and with walks that are not violent, so that it may be purged away; bring about the emptying of the flesh with a sparing diet and reducing measures; have the patient gently rubbed with oil for a long time, so as not to be violently overheated; and it is beneficial to anoint him with ointments that promote sweating and softening, and to have him rest on a soft bed. In those who exercise under unaccustomed exertions, fatigue arises for the following reason: whatever part of the body has not been worked must necessarily have moist flesh in that region, in the particular place unaccustomed to exertion, just as is the case throughout the body of the untrained; so the flesh there must necessarily be dissolved, separated out, and compacted, just as in the case already described. It is advantageous to treat this as follows: use the exercises one is accustomed to, so that the compacted matter, being heated, is thinned and purged away, while the rest of the body is not made moist nor rendered unfit through disuse. Hot baths are beneficial here too, used as before, and rubbing in the same way as before; but there is no need at all for steam-baths, since the exertions themselves are sufficient, by their heat, to thin and purge away the compacted matter. Fatigue arising from one's habitual exercises comes about in this way: from exertion in due measure, no fatigue arises; but when the exertion exceeds the proper occasion, it over-dries the flesh; and once emptied of moisture, the flesh grows hot, aches, shivers, and settles into a fever of some duration, unless properly treated. One should first bathe the patient, not in very much water nor very hot, then, on leaving the bath, give him mild wine to drink, and have him dine on as many and as varied foods as possible, using a great deal of watered drink and mild wine; then have him linger a good while, until the veins, having filled, are raised up; then let him vomit, and after rising, sleep a little, gently; then gradually bring him back to his accustomed food and exertions over six days, and within that time restore him fully to his customary food and drink. The power of this treatment is as follows: a body that has been excessively dried can be restored to moisture without falling into the opposite excess; for if it were possible to know precisely how great the excess of exertion had been, and to remedy it by a corresponding measure of food, that would answer very well; but as it is, this is impossible, while the following is easy: the body, being dried out, when foods of every kind are introduced, each part of the body draws to itself from each food whatever suits it; and once filled and moistened, when the stomach is emptied by vomiting, it releases again whatever excess remains, the empty stomach drawing it back. So the flesh discharges whatever moisture is in excess, but does not release what is in due measure, except by force, exertion, drugs, or some other means of drawing it off. By this gradual approach one restores the body, gently, to its original regimen.
